summary: # Marvelous Designer Tips Sharing: Clothing Details Edition Update P18 ## Introduction In this video, we discuss handling issues related to clothing and model overlap in Marvelous Designer. We focus on the challenges presented by multi-layered clothing and how to resolve conflicts between layers. ## Unstable Areas in Multi-Layered Clothing Sometimes when making multi-layered clothing, there will be unstable areas. In the clothing featured in this video, you can see that it is particularly unstable between the edge and the panel. To address these instabilities, we will utilize several functions: **Reverse Fire**, **Freeze**, and **Hardening**. ### Preparing Panels To make it easier for each panel, turn on random colors first. This dress has three main panels: a large dress panel and two cross-stitches. Use the editor to visualize the relationship between the two panels. One cross-stitch is combined with the outer line of the side panel of the dress, while the other panel sits on top of the two panels, contributing to the outer structure. ## Conflict Resolution Strategy When dealing with multi-layered clothing, we typically address conflicts from the inside out. In this case, I chose the most complete cross-stitch and prepared to apply **Reverse Fire** to it. ### Reverse Fire Options There are two options for Reverse Fire: 1. **Reverse fire the sewing line and the panel**. 2. **Reverse fire only the panel**. In this scenario, I selected both the panel and the sewing line to reverse fire. This way, the sewing line between the panels will not affect the simulation. ## Stabilizing the Simulation After initiating the simulation, you will observe that the previously unstable areas are now stable. Changing the perspective allows us to see that the position of the pleats is very close to the panels. If the panels are too close to each other when using the add function, instability may occur. ### Adjusting Panel Thickness The conflict thickness between the panels is currently set to 1, which is too close. Adjusting it to 2.5 will increase the distance between the panels. Now, switch back to the thick texture surface. ### Hardening Inner Panels Select the inner layer panels. When a panel is hardened, its bending strength is increased, resulting in larger fabric folds. The panel will also slightly open. After this adjustment, using the add function will lead to a more stable configuration and make future adjustments easier. The hardening can then be removed. ## Freezing for Stability To maintain the shape of these panels while keeping them in contact with the outer layer, they still need to be frozen. After starting the simulation, you will notice that these panels do not participate in the simulation and are frozen in the 3D window. ### Managing Hidden Edges In the 2D window, select the hidden edges and press **Shift-Q** to display them, followed by restarting the simulation. After restarting, select "Add" to move the panel to the outer layer according to the powder line. ## Addressing Edge Instabilities Upon starting the simulation, you may find that the edge of the contract remains unstable. Apply Layer 1 to this edge without the application layer. Once applied, simulate again; the higher layer will automatically simulate the outer layer of the lower layer. ### Unlocking and Checking Material Unlock the white panel and change the body to the back to inspect the material's reverse side. The back of the material should be solid black. ## Processing Problematic Areas Examine any problematic areas closely, as they can complicate identification during the simulation. When two plates enter the skirt through the layer to the outer layer, the layer needs to be returned to zero. This adjustment will stabilize the simulation. ### Adjusting the Grid After clicking on a piece of fabric in the 3D window, a small blue dot will appear in both the 3D and 2D windows. Use the selection grid tool to select a portion of the grid near the blue dot in the 2D window and drag the mouse to adjust the positioning. ## Fine-Tuning the Grid Selection Be cautious not to select too much at once, as this can lead to penetrations during adjustments. For smaller selections, use the positioning ball to pull them out. After starting the simulation, the adjusted grid should simulate correctly, allowing for further adjustments. ### Manual Adjustments and Fixing Pins You can manually drag the edge of the grid to fit the inner layer of the skirt. If the grid remains in its previous position after starting the simulation, convert the selected grid to a fixing pin. Open the simulation again to see the applied changes. ## Finalizing the Contract Edge Once the entire grid of the contract edge is on the outside, it will not be worn back in. Delete the existing fixing pin before creating new ones. Harden the outer layer's contract edge and attach it to the inner layer. ### Simulating the Skirt After stabilizing the configuration, simulate the other side of the contract edge. If everything is stable, immediately stop the simulation and complete the hardening process. ## Troubleshooting Instabilities Throughout the simulation, you can continuously press the control button to start or stop the simulation. If instabilities arise, stop the simulation and return to previous points to identify issues. ### Adjusting Conflict Thickness For example, if the conflict thickness of the outer contract edge is not modified to 2.5, it can lead to overlaps and instabilities. Adjust the particle diameter accordingly, and re-simulate to achieve stability. ## Conclusion By carefully managing the thickness, using Reverse Fire, Hardening, and freezing techniques, we can effectively handle conflicts in multi-layered clothing designs. Continue to address any remaining unstable areas with the methods discussed. See you in the next video!
